cases.minimum_complete_submission: ROUND 1 (due 24 Oct, one slide, PDF): one A3/16:9 slide with (a) the data -> features -> model -> agent -> work-order architecture strip (the Mermaid diagram in report Section D.3 collapsed to 7 boxes), (b) a 3-line cleaning/feature approach (train-only regime scaling, rolling mean/std/slope W=20, cap-125 target), (c) model choice with reasoning (IsolationForest + HistGradientBoosting + conformal lower bound; why not LSTM), (d) the Triage Agent rule table (5 severities + escalate_to_human), (e) a one-line dataset-coverage statement (FD001-FD004 by config, regime handling for FD002/4) and (f) one honest number already in hand: FD001 test RMSE 14.2 / NASA score ~310, literature band 11-21 [verified_fact from the prior reproduction]. All four Round-1 items the case PDF names [source_derived_requirement] are covered; only the compression is new work. ROUND 2 (due 13 Dec): a 10-slide PPT/PDF carrying every number + annexed public repo + a recorded clean-clone run. Minimum code that satisfies every Round-2 deliverable the PDF names [source_derived_requirement]: (1) one-command pipeline (`make demo SUBSET=FD001`, config for FD002-FD004 with a per-subset results table), (2) HGBR RUL with official-protocol evaluation (capped and raw RMSE, PHM08 with printed convention) + IsolationForest anomaly, (3) Triage Agent as unit-tested rule table writing SQLite/JSON work orders with escalation and de-dup, (4) MLflow on sqlite backend with aliases, one scripted retrain run whose gate logs accept (and ideally one reject), (5) a 3-4 tab Streamlit dashboard (fleet, engine, work orders, MLflow/retrain log), (6) pinned requirements + lock file, pytest, README with licences. Differentiators in build order after green: conformal intervals with PICP/MPIW, decision-replay A/B/C policy table, feature-drift-triggered retrain with false-alarm count, 'honest metrics' slide. Drop if time runs out: Docker, stream-replay UI, 1D-CNN challenger, cost-sweep.
cases.effort_person_days: Round-1 slide: 1.0-1.5 person-days (content exists; the work is layout, compression and two review passes) [technical_inference]. Round-2 minimum complete (items 1-6 above + deck + recorded run): 13-16 person-days [technical_inference]. Full blueprint (adds CQR intervals, replay harness, drift accept+reject, Docker, four-subset polish): 20-24 person-days. Reasoning: the specialist's 10-11 and the skeptic's 14-18 both assume competent Python engineers; I take the skeptic's figure for the must-haves and add ~25% for two things neither counted: (i) the Round-2 deliverable is a deck plus a recording, so every number must be re-run from a clean clone and screenshot/narrated (1.5-2 days), and (ii) integration debt between MLflow 3 aliases, Evidently 0.7 and Streamlit on a Windows box where streamlit import already fails and pip resolves pandas 3 [verified_fact]. AI coding assistance (Claude Max) removes most boilerplate (loader, tests, Streamlit tabs, Makefile) and I credit it with roughly 20-30% on code-writing time, but it does not shorten training runs, clean-clone rehearsals, or the learning curve of the MLflow registry semantics; the skeptic's '40% light' critique is about those non-typing hours, so AI assistance only partly offsets it [technical_inference]. Compute is not a cost: each subset trains in 1.5-6 min on this CPU [verified_fact].
cases.calendar_feasibility_to_13_dec: Calendar: 6 days to Round 1 (18-24 Oct); a 20-day gap (25 Oct-13 Nov) during which the team does not know whether it is shortlisted (shortlist date unpublished [unverified_assumption]); then a 30-day Round-2 window (14 Nov 10:00 - 13 Dec 23:59 IST) [verified_fact from the Unstop listing, platform-level]. Diwali is ~8 Nov 2026 [unverified_assumption, multiple calendar sites agree], i.e. inside the gap, not the Round-2 window. Indian engineering end-semester exams typically fall in late Nov-Dec [unverified_assumption], so plan on roughly 50% availability during Round 2. Capacity: 3 students x 30 days x ~3 h/day effective = ~34 person-days gross, ~20-25 after exam load; 2 students: ~14-17. Verdict: the 13-16 person-day minimum fits a 3-person team inside the Round-2 window alone with slack, and fits a 2-person team only if the FD001 pipeline, agent and MLflow skeleton are built at risk in the gap (which is low-regret because the same code is needed for Round 3). The full 20-24 day blueprint needs the gap used by a 3-person team. Round 1 is comfortable: 1-1.5 person-days in a 6-day window with the architecture, rule table and reproduced baseline already written. Recommended sequencing: Day 1-2 slide draft; Day 3 lock the environment (fresh venv, pins, FD001 baseline re-run); Day 4-5 slide review + submit by 23 Oct, one day early; gap: FD001 pipeline + agent + MLflow-sqlite skeleton; Round 2 week 1: dashboard + four subsets; week 2: retrain/drift + CQR; week 3: replay harness + clean-clone recording; week 4: deck, 5 MB check, buffer.
cases.critical_path_and_single_points_of_failu: Critical path (serial): environment lock on a fresh venv (streamlit/plotly pin, pandas 2.x pin, MLflow sqlite backend) -> FD001 loader/cleaner/features -> HGBR + official evaluation -> Triage Agent + work orders -> MLflow run/registry -> dashboard -> scripted retrain demo -> clean-clone recorded run -> 10-slide deck. Everything after the environment lock parallelises into three tracks (data/ML, agent+MLOps, dashboard+deck), so the real critical path is the environment lock plus the recorded run at the end. Single points of failure: (1) the one development laptop: no second machine is guaranteed, so a Windows update, disk or OneDrive-sync problem in the last week has no fallback; mitigate with a git remote from day 1 and a Docker/Colab fallback for training. (2) Dependency drift: pip resolves untested pandas 3.0 and streamlit import is currently broken on this machine [verified_fact]; a lock file is the only defence. (3) One teammate owning MLflow registry semantics (sqlite backend, aliases not stages) [verified_fact]; if that person is unavailable during exams the 'MLOps in action' 10% and part of 'working pipeline' 20% are at risk. (4) Deck-size limit (5 MB per Season 3 precedent [unverified_assumption]) if screenshots are not compressed. (5) Dataset host: data.nasa.gov is intermittently unreachable [verified_fact], mitigated by the S3 link, local copy and HF mirror. No hardware, root, kernel or external-service dependency exists, which is why this is the lowest-variance case.
cases.environment_dependencies: Python 3.11+ on Windows 11 (no WSL needed); pinned pandas 2.x, numpy, scikit-learn, mlflow 3.x with `--backend-store-uri sqlite:///mlflow.db`, evidently 0.7.23, river 0.26 (optional), streamlit with a compatible plotly, pytest; all Apache/BSD, free, CPU-only [verified_fact: the stack resolves in pip without conflict]. Known local breakages: streamlit import fails from a plotly mismatch and LightGBM crashed with an access violation on this machine [verified_fact], so LightGBM is out and a fresh venv is mandatory. Data: NASA C-MAPSS zip (12.4 MB, ETag-checked, already on disk) [verified_fact]. Optional: Docker Desktop for the reproducibility story. Deliverable format: PDF/PPTX under ~5 MB [unverified_assumption, Season 3 precedent] plus a public GitHub repo link and a recorded run (judges' ability to run code is unknown, so the recording is mandatory).
cases.rationale: Every input is fixed and already verified: dataset on disk, baseline reproduced four times within 0.4 RMSE, stack resolves, deliverables and weights for both rounds are in the PDF [verified_fact]. The work is the team's declared strength (Python, REST, databases, dashboards) and needs no root, kernel, hardware or lab. The 13-16 person-day minimum fits a 3-person team inside the 30-day Round-2 window even at half availability, and the Round-1 slide is a compression exercise on content that exists. Residual risks are environment fragility (mitigated by pinning) and the deck-first format (mitigated by the recorded run). The main delivery danger is scope creep toward the full blueprint; the must-have/differentiator ordering in Section E is the control. Confidence is high for a complete, credible submission; it is medium for the full differentiated blueprint if the team is two people or does not use the gap.

cases.minimum_complete_submission: ROUND 1 (due 24 Oct, one slide, PDF): the case PDF defines no round deliverables [source_derived_requirement: absent], so the slide must be invented. Minimum credible content: (a) a 6-layer architecture strip (device, edge/router namespace, network/WAN impairment, data, analytics, UI) matching the PDF's required diagram components, (b) the five modules with one-line input/output contracts (classifier with confidence + correction, capacity estimator, policy engine with starvation floors, enforcement via Linux tc HTB+fq_codel+flower, verify-or-rollback loop), (c) the intent API in one line, (d) ONE measured before/after number from the team's own WSL2 testbed: mean RTT under load 638 ms -> 41 ms with bulk at 82% of link, labelled 'WSL2 netns emulation' [verified_fact, measured once by the skeptic on this machine], (e) the three PDF scenarios as the experiment plan, (f) a prototype-vs-production boundary line (CAKE/DSCP/offload, certification). ROUND 2 (due 13 Dec): 10-slide deck + repo + recorded `make demo`. Minimum code that touches all nine 'Expected Output' items [source_derived_requirement]: (1) netns topology script (call, game, 3 TV, bulk, router, wan) with fixed-seed netem; (2) enforcement module: HTB 4-class tree + fq_codel leaves + flower filters, idempotent apply, read-back, reset-to-safe, IPv4 and IPv6; (3) heuristic classifier exposing confidence + /correct endpoint; (4) AIMD capacity estimator with hysteresis scored against the ground-truth netem rate (scenario 2); (5) policy engine with starvation floors and rollback stack; (6) verify module (before/after KPI windows, auto-revert, append-only audit log) plus a watchdog; (7) FastAPI intent endpoint with TTL; (8) dashboard (plain HTML+Chart.js or React polling /metrics) showing latency, jitter, loss, throughput, queue depth, Jain index; (9) experiments harness `make demo SCENARIO=1..3 RUNS=5` producing report.md with medians and bootstrap CIs; (10) setup guide with exact versions, licence list, known-limitations section. Differentiators after green: ML classifier ablation, GitHub Actions re-run, CAKE reference in CI. Drop if short: ML classifier, CAKE comparison, IPv6 scenario runs (keep IPv6 in the enforcement module).
cases.effort_person_days: Round-1 slide: 1.5-2.5 person-days [technical_inference]: 0.5-1 day to re-run and tidy the skeptic's testbed script (already on this machine) so the headline number is the team's own and reproducible, plus 1-1.5 days to design a slide with no PDF template to follow. Round-2 minimum complete (items 1-10): 20-26 person-days [technical_inference]. Full scope (adds ML ablation, CI, CAKE reference, scenario 3 fairness tuning, IPv6 runs): 28-36 person-days. Reasoning: the specialist gave only qualitative sizes (medium/medium-high) and no total; converting them with student rates gives roughly testbed+enforcement 3-4, classifier 1.5-2, estimator with tuning 3-4, policy+rollback+watchdog 2-3, intent API 1, dashboard 2, experiments harness + report 2.5-3, docs/setup guide/licences 1.5-2, deck + recording 2-2.5. The skeptic's measured 82 ms spikes on an idle 40 ms path [verified_fact] mean the estimator's hysteresis will need several tuning iterations, each of which is a 2-3 minute experiment loop that cannot be parallelised or sped up by AI. AI assistance helps strongly with tc command syntax, FastAPI, the dashboard and the report generator (I credit ~25% on code), but the dominant cost here is debugging silently-failing tc semantics, shaping direction, and VM timing noise, which is observation-and-retry time, not typing time. Nobody on the team has demonstrated tc/netns experience [unverified_assumption from the team profile], so I add a 2-3 day learning tax to whichever person owns the kernel side.
cases.calendar_feasibility_to_13_dec: Same calendar as Case 1: 6 days to Round 1, 20-day gap of unknown shortlist status, 30-day Round-2 window overlapping probable end-semester exams [unverified_assumption]. Capacity ~20-25 effective person-days for 3 students in the window, ~14-17 for two. Verdict: the 20-26 person-day minimum does NOT fit inside the Round-2 window alone for either team size at realistic availability; it fits a 3-person team only if the testbed, enforcement and experiments harness (~8-10 person-days) are built at risk during the gap, and it does not fit a 2-person team at all without near full-time work. This matches the prior report's stated flip condition ('two uninterrupted weeks' plus a Linux-networking teammate). Round 1 is feasible but tight: 1.5-2.5 person-days in six days is fine on paper, but one of those days is spent in WSL rather than on the slide, and the slide has no template to anchor it. Sequencing if chosen: Day 1 re-run testbed, capture number and tc output; Day 2-3 slide; Day 4-5 review and submit; gap: topology + enforcement + harness; Round 2 week 1: classifier + estimator; week 2: policy/verify/rollback + intent; week 3: dashboard + scenarios 1-3 at N=5; week 4: docs, recording, deck. There is no slack for an exam week.
cases.critical_path_and_single_points_of_failu: Critical path (serial, because each stage needs the previous one to measure anything): working netns topology with root -> enforcement module verified by read-back -> experiments harness producing a baseline/optimized report -> estimator tuning against ground truth -> verify/rollback loop -> dashboard and intent API -> N=5 repeated runs of all three scenarios -> recorded run -> deck. Only the dashboard, intent API and docs can be done in parallel; the estimator tuning loop is the long pole. Single points of failure: (1) exactly one machine with a verified WSL2 kernel that has netem/htb/fq_codel/ifb/flower; teammates' machines are unverified [unverified_assumption] and every experiment needs root in WSL. (2) WSL2 timing jitter (82 ms max / 12.6 ms mdev idle) [verified_fact] can sink the 'adaptation speed and policy stability' criterion for reasons unrelated to the algorithm; the fallback is a native Ubuntu VM or GitHub Actions, neither of which has been exercised (CAKE-in-CI unconfirmed) [verified_fact]. (3) No sch_cake in the stock kernel [verified_fact], so the production-realistic reference needs CI or a custom kernel. (4) The person who learns tc semantics becomes the only one who can debug the testbed; illness or exams for that person stalls the critical path. (5) Judges cannot run the demo on Windows or without root, so the recorded run and the report.md are the only evidence most assessors will see; a broken recording week is fatal. (6) apt installs (iperf3, irtt, nftables) need network access inside WSL and are not yet present [verified_fact].
cases.environment_dependencies: WSL2 on this laptop (kernel 6.6.87.2, WSL 2.6.1) with root; kernel modules present: sch_htb, sch_netem, sch_fq_codel, ifb, cls_flower, act_mirred [verified_fact]; absent: sch_cake, sch_pie, vcan [verified_fact]. Needs apt: iperf3, iproute2 (present, 6.1.0), irtt (noble package or Go build), optional nftables; Python 3.12 with fastapi, psutil, scikit-learn, optional nfstream 6.6.0 (wheels for cp310-cp313) [verified_fact]. ethtool -K to disable GRO/TSO on veths for stable netem behaviour [technical_inference]. For the headline stability numbers and the CAKE reference: a native Ubuntu VM (Multipass/VirtualBox) or GitHub Actions ubuntu-24.04 with passwordless sudo [verified_fact that sudo is available; CAKE module on that exact runner kernel unconfirmed]. No external dataset required; ISCXVPN2016 optional. Deliverable: PDF/PPTX under ~5 MB [unverified_assumption] plus repo and recording; the PDF additionally demands a setup guide with exact versions and included impairment settings [source_derived_requirement], which is documentation effort Case 1 does not carry.
cases.rationale: The core effect is real and already measured on this exact machine (638 ms -> 41 ms, bulk at 82% of link) [verified_fact], all tools are free and present or apt-installable, and the evidence format is prescribed by the PDF, so a competent submission is possible. But the minimum complete scope is roughly 60% larger than Case 1's (nine mandated outputs, three scenarios with repeated runs, a setup guide), every stage is serial on a single root-enabled WSL machine, estimator tuning is bounded by wall-clock experiment loops that neither AI assistance nor extra people shorten, and no teammate has shown Linux-networking fluency. At realistic student availability during a likely exam period, 20-26 person-days exceeds the Round-2 window unless the gap is used at risk by a 3-person team. Confidence is therefore medium for a complete submission with a 3-person team that starts in the gap, and low for a 2-person team or a team that waits for the shortlist before building.

round1_slide_risk_comparison:
Framing: Round 1 is a single PDF slide on one problem statement, assessed by assessors and a jury, with no published judging criteria beyond the case PDFs [verified_fact, platform-level listing]. Note a source conflict: the Case 1 PDF calls Round 1 a 'design deck' with four named items and seven weighted criteria [source_derived_requirement], while the platform says one slide; plan for one slide that covers all four items and keep a longer version ready in case the portal accepts more pages [technical_inference]. Case 3's PDF has no round structure at all [source_derived_requirement: absent].

CASE 1 slide risk: LOW. Content risk is near zero because the PDF tells the team exactly what to show and how it is weighted (architecture clarity 20%, ML approach 20%, problem understanding 15%, data engineering 15%, MLOps and agent logic 15%, dataset coverage 10%, communication 5%), and every item already exists in the prior report: the 7-box architecture, the cleaning/feature recipe, the model choice with reasons, the Triage rule table, four-subset coverage, and a reproduced FD001 number (RMSE 14.2, score ~310) that few idea-stage slides will carry [verified_fact for the number; hypothesis for competitors]. Effort 1-1.5 person-days leaves 4+ days of review slack. The residual risk is the opposite problem: density. Cramming six weighted items onto one legible page is a layout exercise, and the 'communication quality' criterion punishes a wall of boxes. The strategic risk is crowding: this is the mandated-dataset case with a prescribed deck, so it is the hypothesised modal choice and most slides will show the same LSTM-plus-dashboard architecture [hypothesis]; the slide must make the three differentiators (agent acts on the conformal lower bound, drift-gated retraining with a promotion gate, leakage-audited evaluation) visible in the diagram itself, not in a footnote, or it will read as a competent reproduction. Shortlist-worthiness therefore depends on editorial discipline, which is cheap, not on new work.

CASE 3 slide risk: MEDIUM-HIGH, with a higher ceiling. There is no template, no weights and no named deliverables, so the team must guess what a broadband-practice jury wants from a one-page idea [technical_inference]. The upside is one dramatic, hard-to-fake number (638 ms -> 41 ms mean RTT under load, bulk still at 82% of link) measured on the team's own machine [verified_fact], which is far more memorable on a single page than an RMSE on a dataset with 53 public repos, and the 'verify-or-rollback' loop plus ground-truth-scored capacity estimation is genuinely uncommon [verified_fact for the search]. The downsides: (1) 0.5-1 of the six days goes into re-running the WSL testbed so the number is the team's own and reproducible, time that is not spent on the slide; (2) the PDF asks for six architectural layers, five modules with contracts, three scenarios and a production boundary, which cannot all fit, so the team must choose what to omit with no rubric to guide the cut; (3) judges from a broadband practice will likely know OpenWrt SQM and cake-autorate [technical_inference], so a slide that leads with HTB+fq_codel reads as 'SQM redone' unless the rollback/verification framing is up front; (4) the number must be labelled WSL2 emulation, which weakens it; (5) the specialist never planned a Round-1 artefact for this case, so nothing is pre-written. Effort 1.5-2.5 person-days in six days is feasible, but the variance of the outcome is high: a strong slide is more memorable than Case 1's, a weak one is less convincing than Case 1's.

Net comparison: for a 2-3 person generalist team with six days, Case 1 has the lower risk of producing a shortlist-worthy slide (content fixed, criteria fixed, material written, number reproduced; risk is only compression and standing out in a crowded field). Case 3 has the higher expected memorability per slide but a materially higher chance of an unconvincing or mis-scoped slide, because the team must invent the brief, spend part of the window in WSL, and present an idea whose nearest prior art the jury probably knows. The prior report's flip condition stands: Case 3's slide risk drops to roughly Case 1's level only if a teammate already has tc/netns fluency, because then the testbed day disappears and the slide can be written from experience rather than from the skeptic's script. Whichever case is chosen, submit by 23 Oct to leave one day for portal problems, keep the PDF under 5 MB [unverified_assumption, Season 3 precedent], and remember that the submitted idea becomes Tata Elxsi's property [verified_fact, platform listing], so do not put anything on the slide the team would not hand over.
